records.sentence: The Greek reads ἀπὸ ὀρέων αἰωνίων, "from everlasting mountains."
records.claim: The Greek version of Psalm 76:5 reads ἀπὸ ὀρέων αἰωνίων.
records.explanation: In the Septuagint, which numbers this psalm as 75, verse 5 (corresponding to MT 76:5) reads 'φωτίζεις σὺ θαυμαστῶς ἀπὸ ὀρέων αἰωνίων' (thou shinest wondrously from the everlasting mountains).

records.sentence: Where Hebrew would normally write **הִ**שְׁתּוֹלְלוּ, the psalm writes **אֶ**שְׁתּוֹלְלוּ, with an *aleph* in place of the *he*, an Aramaic habit.
records.claim: This substitution is an Aramaic habit.

evidence.source: Strong's #7997 - Old Testament Hebrew Lexical Dictionary

records.explanation: Grammars identify the substitution of an aleph for the initial he in the hitpa'el/hitpo'el form אשתוללו (for השתוללו) as an Aramaizing feature.

records.sentence: A close parallel in Western art is the climax of Mozart's *Don Giovanni* (1787, libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte).
records.claim: Mozart's *Don Giovanni* dates to 1787 and has a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte.
records.explanation: Mozart's opera 'Don Giovanni' premiered in Prague on October 29, 1787. The libretto was written by Lorenzo Da Ponte.

records.sentence: The libertine has invited to supper the stone statue of the man he killed.
records.claim: Don Giovanni invites the statue of a man he killed to supper.

evidence.source: Don Giovanni | Opera, Cast, Summary, & Facts - Britannica

records.explanation: The plot involves Don Giovanni, a libertine, inviting the stone statue of the Commendatore (whom he had murdered in the opening scene) to dine with him.

records.sentence:
> COMMENDATORE: Dammi la mano in pegno!
> DON GIOVANNI: Eccola! ... Ohimè!
> Che gelo è questo mai!
records.claim: The quoted exchange occurs in Da Ponte's libretto with these speakers and wording.
records.explanation: The text perfectly matches Lorenzo Da Ponte's libretto. The Commendatore demands Don Giovanni's hand, and Don Giovanni reacts with 'Eccola! Ohimè! Che gelo è questo mai!' to the statue's icy grip.

records.sentence: He goes down shouting "No, no, ch'io non mi pento," "No, no, I do not repent."
records.claim: Don Giovanni says the quoted refusal to repent at the end.
records.explanation: The libretto for Mozart's Don Giovanni confirms that Don Giovanni shouts 'No, no, ch'io non mi pento' (No, no, I do not repent) in response to the Commendatore's demands right before he is dragged down to hell.

records.sentence: Most take them as Rashi does: "from the moment You are angry."
records.claim: Most interpreters take the words as Rashi does.
records.explanation: Rashi interprets 'me'az apecha' (מֵאָז אַפֶּךָ) as 'from the time of Your anger' (משעת כעסך). Most other traditional commentators offer a similar explanation, supporting the claim's characterization.

records.sentence: In his piyyut *Lecha Eli Teshukati*, recited in Edot HaMizrach communities after Kol Nidrei, the worshiper confesses: וּמִי יַעֲמֹד לְפָנֶיךָ וּמִי יִהְיֶה תְמוּרָתִי, "and who can stand before You, and who will take my place?"
records.claim: *Lecha Eli Teshukati* is recited in Edot HaMizrach communities after Kol Nidrei.

evidence.source: The liturgical poem sung at his son's funeral... - Ynet News
evidence.quote: For the Sephardim, the piyut opens the prayers of the holy and awesome day

records.explanation: The piyyut Lecha Eli Teshukati is recited before Kol Nidrei in Edot HaMizrach (Sephardic) communities, as it 'opens the prayers of the holy and awesome day,' rather than after Kol Nidrei.
records.suggested_fix: In his piyyut *Lecha Eli Teshukati*, recited in Edot HaMizrach communities before Kol Nidrei, the worshiper confesses: וּמִי יַעֲמֹד לְפָנֶיךָ וּמִי יִהְיֶה תְמוּרָתִי, "and who can stand before You, and who will take my place?"

records.sentence: In his piyyut *Lecha Eli Teshukati*, recited in Edot HaMizrach communities after Kol Nidrei, the worshiper confesses: וּמִי יַעֲמֹד לְפָנֶיךָ וּמִי יִהְיֶה תְמוּרָתִי, "and who can stand before You, and who will take my place?"
records.claim: Ibn Ezra's *Lecha Eli Teshukati* contains the quoted confession.
records.explanation: The quoted Hebrew line ('ומי יעמד לפניך ומי יהיה תמורתי') is indeed found in the confession section of Ibn Ezra's Lecha Eli Teshukati.

records.sentence: The piyyut's expects *not I*, and it immediately begins the alphabetical confession.
records.claim: An alphabetical confession begins immediately after the quoted question in the piyyut.

evidence.source: מהו הפיוט לך אלי תשוקתי ולמה אומרים אותו לפני כל נדרי?- Kaparot.org.il
evidence.quote: ומי יעמד לפניך ומי יהיה תמורתי ואיך חשבון לך אתן ואיך אצדק בטענתי ואשמתי וארבתי ובגדתי

records.explanation: The alphabetical confession does not begin immediately after the quoted question. There is an intervening line ('And how shall I give You an account, and how shall I be justified in my plea?') before the alphabetical list of sins begins.
records.suggested_fix: The piyyut's expects *not I*, and it then begins the alphabetical confession.

records.sentence: Tukaram, the seventeenth-century saint-poet of Maharashtra, wrote in the devotional *abhang* form for the Varkari pilgrims of the god Vitthal.
records.claim: Tukaram was a seventeenth-century Maharashtra saint-poet associated with the abhang form and Varkari devotion to Vitthal.
records.explanation: Tukaram was a renowned 17th-century Marathi saint-poet of the Bhakti movement who composed abhangs for the Varkari pilgrims devoted to Vitthal.

records.sentence: He tied holiness to the same test:
records.claim: The following Marathi lines are attributable to Tukaram.
records.explanation: The lines correspond to Abhanga 204 of Tukaram's Gatha ('Je ka ranjale gaanjale...'), which is widely attributed to him.

records.sentence:
"Those who are tormented and oppressed —
> whoever calls them his own,
> know him to be the true saint;
> know that God is right there."
records.claim: The English passage fairly translates the four Marathi lines attributed to Tukaram.
records.explanation: The English translation provided faithfully captures the meaning of Tukaram's Marathi lines 'Je ka ranjale gaanjale...', where he identifies true saintliness and the presence of God with those who care for the oppressed.

records.sentence: The Greek translator heard a different verb altogether: ἑορτάσει σοι, "shall keep festival to You."
records.claim: The Greek Psalter reads ἑορτάσει σοι at Psalm 75:11 in its numbering.

evidence.quote: In the slightly different numbering system of the Greek Septuagint version of the bible, and in the Latin Vulgate, this psalm is Psalm 75... 76:10 Ὅτι ἐνθύμιον ἀνθρώπου ἐξομολογήσεταί σοι, καὶ ἐγκατάλειμμα ἐνθυμίου ἑορτάσει σοι.

records.explanation: The Septuagint numbers this as Psalm 75, and its verse 11 (sometimes numbered 10 depending on superscription inclusion) reads exactly ἑορτάσει σοι.

records.sentence: That means reading תָּחֹג, "celebrate," for תַּחְגֹּר, "gird," and the remnant of fury becomes a festival crowd.
records.claim: The proposed Hebrew reading תָּחֹג accurately represents the alleged Greek translator's textual basis.

evidence.quote: Ewald, like the lxx, reads תּחגּך, ἑορτάσει σοι, in connection with which... Possibly we should render, 'and those who remain from their wrath shall celebrate a festival,' since the suggested emendation is the word used in that sense.

records.explanation: The Masoretic text uses the verb תַּחְגֹּר (gird), while the Greek translation implies a back-translated Hebrew root of חגג (celebrate), often proposed by scholars as תָּחֹג (or similar forms).

records.sentence: But later synagogue reading makes the connection easy to hear, since Zechariah 14 is read on the same first day of Sukkot on which this psalm is sung.
records.claim: Zechariah 14 is the first-day Sukkot haftarah, and Psalm 76 is sung on that day in a later synagogue custom.

evidence.quote: This psalm is recited on the first day of Sukkot.
The haftarah for the first day of Sukkot is the last chapter of the book of Zechariah.

records.explanation: Zechariah 14 is indeed the Haftarah for the first day of Sukkot, and Psalm 76 is designated as the Psalm of the Day (Shir Shel Yom) for the first day of Sukkot in various traditions (such as that of the Vilna Gaon).

records.sentence: Proposed corrections that read "Edom" for אָדָם or the city Hamath for חֲמַת are clever and unnecessary.
records.claim: Edom and Hamath have actually been proposed as alternative readings by textual interpreters.

evidence.source: The 1979 Book of Common Prayer / Reddit Episcopalian discussion
evidence.quote: 1979 BCP: Truly, wrathful Edom will give you thanks, and the remnant of Hamath will keep your feast... adam and edom can be spelled with the same letters, just with different vowel marks

records.explanation: Modern textual interpreters, and translations such as the 1979 Book of Common Prayer, have proposed emending the Hebrew 'adam' and 'hamat' to the proper nouns Edom and Hamath.

records.sentence: Two independent compositions place יִבְצֹר רוּחַ נְגִידִים beside Isaiah 63's warrior מִבָּצְרָה... חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים, "crimsoned in garments from Bozrah" (Isa 63:1): the Ashkenazi Rosh Hashanah *yotzer* and a Hasidic Shabbat *zemer* that names both Edom and Bozrah (quoted in the liturgical section).
records.claim: An Ashkenazi Rosh Hashanah yotzer places the Psalm 76 phrase alongside language from Isaiah 63.

evidence.source: תולדות: בבואו מאדום - על מה שהיה ועל מה שקורה
evidence.quote: "בבואו מאדום חמוץ בגדים. זבח לו בבצרה וטבח לו בבוגדים. ויז נצחם מלבושיו להאדים. ובכחו הגדול יבצור רוח נגידים..." קטע הפיוט הזה, בית מתוך "ברוך ה' יום יום" שהוא חלק מזמירות השבת ברוב סידורי התפילה האשכנזיים, הוא פרפראזה על נבואתו הקשה של ישעיהו: "מי זה בא מאדום, חמוץ בגדים מבצרה..."

records.explanation: The author mistakenly split a single composition into two. The Ashkenazi Shabbat zemer 'Baruch Hashem Yom Yom' (written by R. Shimon bar Yitzchak, who also famously wrote Ashkenazi Rosh Hashanah yotzrot) is the single composition that places the Psalm 76 phrase alongside Isaiah 63's 'Bozrah' and 'crimsoned garments'. There is no separate Ashkenazi Rosh Hashanah yotzer that does this.
records.suggested_fix: A single composition places יִבְצֹר רוּחַ נְגִידִים beside Isaiah 63's warrior מִבָּצְרָה... חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים, "crimsoned in garments from Bozrah" (Isa 63:1): an Ashkenazi Shabbat *zemer* that names both Edom and Bozrah (quoted in the liturgical section).

records.sentence: Two independent compositions place יִבְצֹר רוּחַ נְגִידִים beside Isaiah 63's warrior מִבָּצְרָה... חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים, "crimsoned in garments from Bozrah" (Isa 63:1): the Ashkenazi Rosh Hashanah *yotzer* and a Hasidic Shabbat *zemer* that names both Edom and Bozrah (quoted in the liturgical section).
records.claim: A separate Hasidic Shabbat zemer names Edom and Bozrah and places them alongside the Psalm 76 phrase.

evidence.source: תולדות: בבואו מאדום - על מה שהיה ועל מה שקורה
evidence.quote: "בבואו מאדום חמוץ בגדים. זבח לו בבצרה וטבח לו בבוגדים. ויז נצחם מלבושיו להאדים. ובכחו הגדול יבצור רוח נגידים..." קטע הפיוט הזה, בית מתוך "ברוך ה' יום יום" שהוא חלק מזמירות השבת ברוב סידורי התפילה האשכנזיים, הוא פרפראזה על נבואתו הקשה של ישעיהו: "מי זה בא מאדום, חמוץ בגדים מבצרה..."

records.explanation: As noted above, there are not 'two independent compositions', and the zemer is not specifically a separate Hasidic composition, but rather the standard medieval Ashkenazi Shabbat zemer 'Baruch Hashem Yom Yom' (which is sung across both Hasidic and non-Hasidic Ashkenazi communities).
records.suggested_fix: A single composition places יִבְצֹר רוּחַ נְגִידִים beside Isaiah 63's warrior מִבָּצְרָה... חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים, "crimsoned in garments from Bozrah" (Isa 63:1): an Ashkenazi Shabbat *zemer* that names both Edom and Bozrah (quoted in the liturgical section).

records.sentence: On 1 June 1679, an outlawed field-meeting of Scottish Covenanters near Loudoun Hill saw government dragoons under John Graham of Claverhouse riding toward them.
records.claim: The described Covenanter encounter took place on 1 June 1679.

evidence.quote: The Battle of Drumclog was fought on 1 June 1679 during the Covenanter rebellion of 1679. Rebel Covenanters defeated a Scots Army force under John Graham of Claverhouse

records.explanation: Historical records indicate the Battle of Drumclog between the Scottish Covenanters and government dragoons occurred precisely on 1 June 1679.

records.sentence: On 1 June 1679, an outlawed field-meeting of Scottish Covenanters near Loudoun Hill saw government dragoons under John Graham of Claverhouse riding toward them.
records.claim: The encounter began at an outlawed Covenanter field-meeting near Loudoun Hill.

evidence.quote: A large conventicle was planned to take place at Loudoun Hill, on the boundary of Ayrshire and Lanarkshire, in defiance of government persecution of the Covenanters... when it was reported that Scots Army dragoons under John Graham of Claverhouse were heading to the area.

records.explanation: The encounter (leading to the Battle of Drumclog) originated at an illegal conventicle (field-meeting) held by Covenanters near Loudoun Hill.

records.sentence: On 1 June 1679, an outlawed field-meeting of Scottish Covenanters near Loudoun Hill saw government dragoons under John Graham of Claverhouse riding toward them.
records.claim: Government dragoons approaching the meeting were under John Graham of Claverhouse.

evidence.quote: A large conventicle was planned to take place at Loudoun Hill, on the boundary of Ayrshire and Lanarkshire, in defiance of government persecution of the Covenanters. On the morning of Sunday 1 June... it was reported that the dragoons of Claverhouse were heading to the area.

records.explanation: Historical sources confirm that on June 1, 1679, a Covenanter field-meeting near Loudoun Hill was approached by dragoons commanded by John Graham of Claverhouse.

records.sentence: Covenanter tradition remembers that before engaging, they sang Psalm 76 in the Scottish metrical version:
records.claim: Covenanter tradition records the group singing Psalm 76 before this engagement.

evidence.quote: It was on a Sabbath morning on June 1st, 1679, that a conventicle there was surprised by a strong body of troops under Claverhouse... Immediately the fighting men separated themselves from the rest of the worshippers, and, setting themselves in order, marched down the hill to join issue with the enemy, singing, as they went, Psalm 76...

records.explanation: Tradition and historical accounts state that the Covenanters sang Psalm 76 as they marched to meet Claverhouse's troops.

records.sentence: Covenanter tradition remembers that before engaging, they sang Psalm 76 in the Scottish metrical version:
records.claim: The version reportedly sung was the Scottish metrical Psalm 76.

evidence.quote: singing, as they went, Psalm 76 to the tune Martyrs : In Judah's land God is well known...

records.explanation: The lyrics sung were those of the 1650 Scottish Metrical Psalter.

records.sentence:
In Judah's land God is well known,
his name's in Israel great:
In Salem is his tabernacle,
in Sion is his seat.
records.claim: These four lines reproduce the Scottish metrical version attributed to the Covenanters.

evidence.quote:
In Judah's land God is well known,
His name's in Isr'el great :
In Salem is his tabernacle,
In Sion is his seat.

records.explanation: The quoted lines accurately reproduce the Scottish Metrical Psalter version of Psalm 76. (Minor spelling variations such as Israel for Isr'el are acceptable modernizations or metrical expansions.)

records.sentence: Then they charged and routed the dragoons.
records.claim: The Covenanters charged and routed the dragoons after the reported singing.

evidence.quote: That was their victory song, for soon Clavers and his men were discomfited and in flight.

records.explanation: Historical records of the Battle of Drumclog confirm that the Covenanters successfully charged and routed Claverhouse's dragoons.

records.sentence: For these men, persecuted by a king who claimed authority over their church, the psalm's promise that God "prunes the spirit of princes" was a political creed.
records.claim: The Covenanters in this episode were persecuted under a king who claimed authority over their church.

evidence.quote: They signed this Covenant to confirm their opposition to the interference by the Stuart kings in the affairs of the Presbyterian Church of Scotland... they also believed that they were the spiritual heads of the Church of Scotland. This latter belief could not be accepted by the [Covenanters]... The persecutions became more frequent and cruel on the Restoration of Charles II in 1660.

records.explanation: The Covenanters faced severe persecution precisely because they rejected the Stuart kings' (Charles II) claims of Royal Supremacy over the Church.

records.sentence: For these men, persecuted by a king who claimed authority over their church, the psalm's promise that God "prunes the spirit of princes" was a political creed.
records.claim: These Covenanters treated Psalm 76’s final verse as a political creed.

evidence.source: Jardine's Book of Martyrs - John Leslie duke of Rothes
evidence.quote: Shields also mentioned that his transportation to Scotland was delayed due to the King's death 'by His Order, who cuts of the Spirit of Princes, and is Terrible to the Kings of the Earth'.

records.explanation: Covenanter literature explicitly applied the final verse of Psalm 76 (regarding God cutting off the spirit of princes) to their struggle against the Stuart monarchy, functioning as a theological and political creed.
